title: Preparation of Potassium Ferric Oxalate
objective: Prepare ferrous oxalate as an intermediate, then oxidise it to the ferric complex
Combine with potassium oxalate to form K3[Fe(C2O4)3]·3H2O
Explain why the product must be protected from light during preparation and storage
Calculate the percentage yield of the emerald-green crystalline product

theory.statement: Potassium trioxalatoferrate(III), K3[Fe(C2O4)3]·3H2O, is a complex salt — its complex ion [Fe(C2O4)3]3- survives intact in solution, unlike a double salt. It is prepared by first forming ferrous oxalate, oxidising it with hydrogen peroxide in the presence of excess potassium oxalate, and crystallising the emerald-green product.
theory.derivationNote: Fe2+ + C2O4^2- → FeC2O4 (yellow precipitate); this is then oxidised: 2FeC2O4 + H2O2 + 4K2C2O4 (excess) → 2K3[Fe(C2O4)3] + 2KOH, with excess oxalate present throughout to complex the Fe3+ as it forms, rather than letting it hydrolyse to Fe(OH)3. The finished complex is PHOTOSENSITIVE: light reduces Fe3+ to Fe2+ within the complex, releasing CO2 and slowly decomposing the emerald-green product — the same photochemistry once used in blueprint (cyanotype-related) processes.
keyEquations: K3[Fe(C2O4)3] --light--> photoreduction (Fe3+ → Fe2+, loss of CO2)

apparatus.name: Ferrous ammonium sulphate
apparatus.spec: Mohr's salt, as the iron source
apparatus.why: Provides Fe2+ to form the initial ferrous oxalate

apparatus.name: Oxalic acid / potassium oxalate
apparatus.why: Precipitates ferrous oxalate, and (in excess) complexes the Fe3+ formed

apparatus.name: Hydrogen peroxide
apparatus.why: Oxidises Fe2+ to Fe3+ within the oxalate system

apparatus.name: Dark/amber bottle or paper wrapping
apparatus.why: Protects the finished, light-sensitive product from photodecomposition

procedure.text: Dissolve ferrous ammonium sulphate and precipitate ferrous oxalate by adding oxalic acid solution.
Filter and wash the yellow ferrous oxalate precipitate.
Add potassium oxalate solution to the moist precipitate, then add hydrogen peroxide slowly with stirring, keeping the mixture warm.
Add a further small amount of oxalic acid to dissolve any remaining ferric hydroxide, then filter hot.
Evaporate in subdued light or wrapped from light, then cool to crystallise.
Filter, dry in the dark, weigh, and calculate the percentage yield.

steps: Precipitate ferrous oxalate, then oxidise with H2O2 in excess oxalate

expectedResult.quantity: Percentage yield of potassium ferric oxalate
expectedResult.statement: Oxidising ferrous oxalate with hydrogen peroxide in the presence of excess potassium oxalate, then crystallising in subdued light, gives emerald-green K3[Fe(C2O4)3]·3H2O crystals; exposure to bright light during preparation measurably lowers the yield of pure product through photoreduction.

safety: Hydrogen peroxide can bleach skin — avoid contact.
Oxalates are toxic if ingested — wash hands after handling.
sourcesOfError: Working in bright light photoreduces the product as it forms, lowering yield and purity.
Insufficient excess oxalate lets some Fe3+ hydrolyse to Fe(OH)3 instead of complexing.
Evaporating too far concentrates and darkens the solution, making the crystallising point hard to judge.

viva.question: Why must potassium ferric oxalate be protected from light?
viva.expectedConcept: Light photochemically reduces the Fe3+ in the complex to Fe2+, with loss of CO2, slowly decomposing the emerald-green complex. This is why the preparation and storage are done in subdued light or a dark container.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking light simply fades the colour without any chemical change occurring.

viva.question: Why is excess potassium oxalate present during the oxidation step?
viva.expectedConcept: As Fe2+ is oxidised to Fe3+, the excess oxalate immediately complexes it as [Fe(C2O4)3]3-. Without enough oxalate present, the Fe3+ would instead hydrolyse to insoluble, gelatinous Fe(OH)3, which is lost from the desired product.
viva.answerLogic: Complexation competes with, and must outrun, hydrolysis.
viva.commonMisconception: Adding the oxidiser before ensuring enough oxalate is present.

viva.question: Is potassium ferric oxalate a double salt or a complex salt? How would you tell experimentally?
viva.expectedConcept: It is a complex salt: in solution, its complex ion [Fe(C2O4)3]3- does not show the free, simple Fe3+ test reactions (e.g. no red colour with KSCN), because the iron is bound within the complex rather than existing as a simple aquo ion.
viva.answerLogic: Absence of simple-ion reactions distinguishes a complex from a double salt.
viva.commonMisconception: Assuming any coloured crystalline salt combining two components must be a double salt.

preLab.question: Potassium ferric oxalate is best described as a:
preLab.feedback: Its complex ion [Fe(C2O4)3]3- survives dissolution intact, the defining feature of a complex salt.

duringLab.question: Complete at least one preparation and weigh the product.

postLab.question: Working in bright light during this preparation will:
options: Change the product's formula only, not its yield
postLab.feedback: Light reduces Fe3+ within the complex, decomposing product as it forms and lowering the yield of pure crystals.

expectedBehaviour: Emerald-green crystals; yield falls if not protected from light
